1969 Ford Cobra Has the Great Original Ram Air 428 and Low Price, No One Cares It's a 1-of-1
12 photos
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Dale Baliles
Have we really reached the point where a genuine, factory-documented 1969 Ford Cobra with its matching-numbers 428 Cobra Jet V8 can sit on the market for two weeks without someone snatching it up? That is the exact scenario unfolding right now in Winchester, Virginia, where a seller has listed an original R-code fastback on a flatbed trailer for $22,500 or best offer, complete with a clean title and a bonus parts car.
To be fair, the 99,999 miles shown in the listing is just an online placeholder, and nobody is pretending this Blue Oval bruiser is ready for the local cruise night tonight. Still, the bones are mouthwatering for any blue-blooded gearhead: a factory R-code 428 Cobra Jet Ram Air engine paired with a 4-speed manual transmission, a tough 3.50:1 nodular-iron Traction-Lok rear axle, power steering, and power front disc brakes.
There are a few names in the car-verse that have the gravitas of a neutron star (only the densest cosmic object known to science, after the zero-volume-infinite-density black hole mind-wrecker), and Cobra Jet is one of those heavyweights. The legendary Ford motor is probably most associated with Mustangs – for some reason, people tend to forget about the Blue Oval’s mid-size killer, the Cobra.
This is probably one of history’s most offensive injustices, since the 1969 Ford Fairlane Torino Talladega won 29 races in NASCAR. Ironically, the aerodynamic Talladega didn’t win the inaugural Talladega 500 race, where the Dodge Charger Daytona debuted. The controversy looms to this day whether Ma Mopar sweet-talked Bill France, the boss of NASCAR, into pulling some strings to puppeteer the Chrysler onto the highest step of the podium for a perfect introduction of the new model.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Dale Baliles No matter what happened on the track that day, the 1969 championship went to Ford. On the street, however, the dispute was much heated, with Dodge’s Charger R/T and Ford’s Cobra taking turns at punching each other with every stoplight opportunity they got. Eventually, the Mopar got the upper hand, selling nearly 4,500 more cars than the FoMoCo muscle car (19,298 versus 14,885).
The big irony of it was that the Cobra didn’t get the Boss 429 engine, which was also launched in 1969 specifically for NASCAR homologation. Picture this: the NASCAR car didn’t get the NASCAR engine on the street. The Mustang Boss 429 did – which wasn’t running it in NASCAR. The Ford Cobra ran with the 428 Cobra Jet for civilian use. It was the only engine offered in the bare-bones muscle car, but it could be optioned with the Ram Air function, for 113 extra bucks.
Now back to the car in this story – and gallery. A closer look at it strapped onto its trailer reveals why it takes a brave soul with a well-equipped garage to step up. Its factory Indian Fire red paint has faded into a chalky, sun-baked patina, and both the front windshield and the sweeping fastback rear glass are completely gone. There is a noticeable dent in the driver's door, and the rear bumper wears plenty of surface rust.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Dale Baliles Despite the rough edges, the overall body lines look remarkably straight, the quad-headlight grille and front bumper are intact, and the hooded scoop with its factory hold-down pins still commands respect. The car currently sits on aftermarket 5-slot mag wheels rather than its original 14-inch Argent styled steel wheels. Inside, a thick coat of dust covers the four-pod instrument cluster, the factory tachometer, and the original three-spoke steering wheel.
Piled with a silver tarp and a blanket, the cabin still retains its black vinyl bucket seats, even if the passenger cushion has a split seam, alongside the center console and 4-speed shifter. Under the cut-out hood sits the matching-numbers 428 V8 wearing finned aluminum valve covers and an aftermarket open-element air cleaner. Better yet, the deal includes a 1969 Torino GT 302 automatic parts car with intact glass.
Understanding why a project like this matters requires looking back at the muscle car wars of the late 1960s. When Plymouth shook up the industry in 1968 with the stripped-down, budget-priced Road Runner street bruiser, Dodge quickly followed with the Super Bee, while Pontiac prepared its brash GTO Judge for 1969. Buyers clearly wanted maximum horsepower in an intermediate body without paying extra money for plush interior trim and heavy luxury add-ons.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Dale Baliles Ford answered that call in 1969 by borrowing the iconic Cobra name it had acquired from Carroll Shelby and slapping it onto a stripped-down Fairlane intermediate chassis. Marketed simply as the Cobra, without Fairlane or Torino sobriquets, this one-year-only model came in two body styles: a formal two-door hardtop with a $3,206 base price and a sleek two-door SportsRoof fastback starting at $3,189, undercutting fancier rivals while putting every single dollar into pure street performance.
Every 1969 Cobra left the factory with serious firepower under the hood. The base powerplant was the Q-code 428-cubic-inch four-barrel Cobra Jet V8 without functional hood induction, while stepping up to the optional R-code 428-cubic-inch Cobra Jet Ram Air V8 added a functional scoop that force-fed cool air into the carburetor. A heavy-duty 4-speed manual transmission was standard equipment, and a rugged 3-speed SelectShift Cruise-O-Matic automatic transmission was also optional.
Fitted with 10.6:1 compression and a 735-cfm Holley carburetor, both the Q-code and R-code 428 engines were conservatively rated at 335 horsepower at 5,200 rpm and 440 lb-ft of torque at 3,400 rpm. Ordering a 3.91:1 or 4.30:1 rear axle brought Super Cobra Jet internals. Period tests clocked the Cobra from 0 to 60 mph in 7.3 seconds and through the quarter-mile in 14.9 seconds at 95.2 mph, with tops speeds in the vicinity of 125 mph.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Dale Baliles Despite that blistering pace, overall 1969 Cobra production remained relatively modest, split between 3,786 hardtops and 11,099 fastbacks. According to the Marti Report included with this Winchester car, this Indian Fire example was ordered on September 6, 1968, and built at the Lorain, Ohio plant on November 12, 1968, running 35 days behind schedule before selling at Bristol Ford in Pennsylvania on February 19, 1969.
That same Marti Report breaks down just how special this particular SportsRoof truly is. Out of all the 1969 Cobra SportsRoofs built, 7,454 had the R-code 428 Cobra Jet Ram Air, with 3,910 of them carrying a close-ratio 4-speed manual transmission. The numbers drop abruptly after that: only 175 put on the Indian Fire war paint and the black vinyl bucket seats.
If we really want to nitpick the numbers, we can – this is a one-of-one, if we account for the white sidewalls, Argent steelies, and remote-controlled left mirror. But that’s just like saying it’s the only one built by a man named Joe wearing a red hat and a goatee and size 8 shoes.
Let’s keep it real. It’s a rare muscle car, it still has the numbers-matching big-block, and it takes plenty of elbow grease to bring back. Well, that, and $22,500 (with the donor Torino included) – a number that, for some reason, seems to fend off buyers. But why?
